Savannah Truck Accident Lawyers — Aggressive Advocacy After Catastrophic Collisions

Savannah sits at the crossroads of two of the Southeast's busiest freight corridors, and the consequences are measured in shattered lives. When a fully loaded tractor-trailer weighing up to 80,000 pounds collides with a passenger vehicle, the injuries are rarely minor — they are catastrophic, life-altering, and often fatal.

Roden Law has recovered more than $300 million for injured clients across Georgia and South Carolina. The Savannah office team understands the unique trucking dangers facing Chatham County residents, and the firm brings the resources, investigative depth, and trial willingness needed to hold negligent trucking companies accountable.

If you or a family member has been injured in a truck accident in Savannah or surrounding Southeast Georgia, call (912) 303-5850 for a free consultation. Roden Law handles every truck accident case on a contingency fee basis — there are no attorney fees unless the case is won.

Why Savannah Is a Truck Accident Hotspot

Savannah is not just a historic coastal city — it is one of the most active freight hubs in the United States. The Port of Savannah, operated by the Georgia Ports Authority, is the busiest single-terminal container port in North America and the third-busiest port in the country overall. Every year, millions of container units move through the port and onto Georgia's highways aboard thousands of tractor-trailers.

The consequences for local roadways are significant. Interstate 16 connects Savannah to Macon and Atlanta, functioning as a primary east-west freight artery that channels port traffic deep into the state. Interstate 95, the major north-south corridor along the Eastern Seaboard, passes directly through Chatham County. Together, these two interstates funnel an estimated 15,000 or more commercial trucks per day through the Savannah metropolitan area.

Beyond the interstates, secondary roads bear a heavy burden as well. Jimmy DeLoach Parkway serves as a direct connector between the port and I-95, carrying a concentrated stream of container trucks through the rapidly developing Pooler industrial corridor. Warehousing and distribution centers along this stretch continue to expand, adding more truck traffic to roads that were not originally designed for such volume.

Seasonal patterns make the danger worse. Holiday freight surges in the fall and winter dramatically increase truck volume, while agricultural shipments from South Georgia — including Vidalia onions, pecans, and timber — add heavy loads to I-16 during harvest months. These peaks coincide with higher passenger vehicle traffic, creating a dangerous combination on already congested highways. For Savannah residents, the risk of a serious truck collision is not abstract — it is a daily reality of living in one of America's busiest port cities.

Who Is Liable in a Savannah Truck Accident?

Truck accident cases are fundamentally different from standard car accident claims in Savannah because multiple parties may share legal responsibility. Identifying every liable party is critical to maximizing the compensation available to injured victims.

The Truck Driver

Driver negligence remains the most common cause of truck accidents. This includes fatigued driving in violation of federal Hours of Service regulations, distracted driving, driving under the influence, speeding, and aggressive lane changes. When a driver violates federal safety rules, that violation can serve as powerful evidence of negligence.

The Trucking Company

Under the legal doctrine of respondeat superior, a trucking company is liable for the negligent acts of its drivers committed within the scope of employment. Beyond vicarious liability, trucking companies can be held directly liable for negligent hiring, training, retention, and supervision. Companies that fail to screen drivers for poor safety records, skip required drug and alcohol testing, or pressure drivers to exceed legal driving hours bear direct responsibility for the crashes that result.

Cargo Loading Companies

Third-party companies responsible for loading freight can be liable when overloaded or improperly secured cargo causes a truck to become unstable, shift during transit, or spill onto the roadway. Federal regulations set strict weight limits and securement standards — violations create liability.

Vehicle and Parts Manufacturers

When a mechanical defect causes or contributes to a crash, the manufacturer of the truck or the defective component may be liable under Georgia product liability law. Brake failures, tire blowouts, defective coupling devices, and steering system malfunctions are among the most common equipment-related causes of truck accidents.

The Role of Federal Regulations

The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) enforces comprehensive safety regulations under 49 CFR Parts 390 through 399 that govern nearly every aspect of commercial trucking. Violations of these regulations — whether related to driver qualifications, vehicle maintenance, cargo securement, or hours of service — are not merely administrative infractions. In a Georgia courtroom, FMCSA violations serve as compelling evidence that a trucking company or driver failed to meet the minimum standard of care required by law.

Common Types of Truck Accidents in Savannah

The size, weight, and configuration of commercial trucks create accident patterns that are distinct from passenger vehicle collisions. Roden Law's truck accident attorneys handle every type of commercial vehicle crash, including:

  • Jackknife accidents — The trailer swings outward at an acute angle to the cab, often sweeping across multiple lanes of traffic on I-16 or I-95.
  • Underride and override accidents — A passenger vehicle slides beneath the trailer of a truck, frequently resulting in fatal or catastrophic head and neck injuries.
  • Wide-turn accidents — Trucks making right turns swing into adjacent lanes, crushing vehicles alongside them, particularly at Savannah's downtown intersections.
  • Rear-end collisions — A loaded truck traveling at highway speed requires up to 40 percent more stopping distance than a passenger vehicle, making rear-end crashes devastatingly forceful.
  • Blind spot accidents — Commercial trucks have massive blind spots along both sides, the front, and the rear. Lane-change collisions on I-95 are a frequent result.
  • Rollover accidents — Hazardous materials trucks and tanker trucks are especially vulnerable to rollovers on curved highway ramps and exit lanes.
  • 18-wheeler and semi-truck collisions — The most common type of catastrophic truck accident, involving the largest and heaviest vehicles on the road.

Georgia Truck Accident Laws

Truck accident claims in Savannah are governed by Georgia state law as well as federal trucking regulations. Understanding both legal frameworks is essential to building a successful case.

Statute of Limitations

Under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33, Georgia imposes a two-year statute of limitations for personal injury claims arising from truck accidents. The clock begins running on the date of the accident. If a victim dies from truck accident injuries, the wrongful death statute of limitations is also two years from the date of death under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33. Failing to file a lawsuit within this window forfeits the right to seek compensation entirely. Given the complexity of truck accident investigations, contacting an attorney promptly is critical.

Georgia's Modified Comparative Fault Rule

Georgia follows a modified comparative fault system under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33. An injured person can recover damages only if their own percentage of fault is less than 50 percent. If the injured person is found to be 50 percent or more at fault, recovery is barred completely. When fault is below that threshold, the damages award is reduced by the plaintiff's percentage of fault. Trucking companies and their insurers routinely attempt to shift blame onto the injured motorist — experienced legal representation is essential to defeating these tactics.

Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations

The FMCSA's regulations under 49 CFR Parts 390 through 399 establish mandatory safety standards for the commercial trucking industry. Key regulations that frequently arise in Savannah truck accident cases include:

  • Hours of Service (HOS) rules (49 CFR Part 395) — Drivers of property-carrying vehicles may drive a maximum of 11 hours after 10 consecutive hours off duty, within a 14-hour on-duty window. Violations of these limits are a leading cause of fatigue-related truck accidents.
  • Electronic Logging Device (ELD) mandate — Since 2017, most commercial trucks are required to use ELDs to electronically record driving hours, replacing paper logbooks that were easily falsified.
  • Vehicle maintenance and inspection standards (49 CFR Parts 393 and 396) — Trucking companies must conduct regular inspections, maintain detailed maintenance records, and ensure vehicles meet minimum safety standards before operating on public roads.
  • Driver qualification standards (49 CFR Part 391) — Requirements for medical fitness, driving history review, drug and alcohol testing, and commercial driver's license qualifications.

Evidence Preservation

Truck accident evidence is perishable. Electronic control module (ECM) data — commonly called the truck's "black box" — records speed, braking, and engine performance in the moments before a crash but may be overwritten within days. Driver logs, ELD data, GPS records, dash cam footage, weigh station reports, and vehicle maintenance records are all subject to routine destruction under company retention policies. Sending a spoliation letter demanding preservation of this evidence is one of the first and most critical steps in any truck accident case.

Filing in Chatham County

Truck accident lawsuits arising from crashes in the Savannah area are typically filed in Chatham County Superior Court. Roden Law's attorneys regularly practice in this court and understand the local procedures, judges, and litigation dynamics that affect case strategy and outcomes.

Truck Accident Injuries Are More Severe

The sheer physics of a collision between an 80,000-pound commercial truck and a 4,000-pound passenger vehicle produce injuries that are dramatically more severe than those in typical motor vehicle accidents. Truck accident victims in Savannah frequently suffer:

  • Traumatic brain injuries (TBI) — Ranging from concussions to severe diffuse axonal injuries that cause permanent cognitive impairment.
  • Spinal cord injuries and paralysis — Complete or incomplete spinal cord damage resulting in paraplegia or quadriplegia, requiring lifelong medical care.
  • Amputations and crush injuries — The force of a truck collision can destroy limbs beyond surgical repair.
  • Severe burn injuries — Particularly in accidents involving fuel tank ruptures, hazardous materials, or post-collision fires.
  • Multiple fractures and internal organ damage — Broken bones, ruptured organs, and internal bleeding requiring emergency surgery and extended hospitalization.
  • Wrongful death — Truck accidents are disproportionately fatal. Surviving family members may pursue wrongful death claims under Georgia law.

The medical costs associated with these injuries are staggering. A single traumatic brain injury can generate millions of dollars in lifetime treatment, rehabilitation, and lost earning capacity. Roden Law works with medical experts, life care planners, and vocational economists to ensure that every component of a client's damages is fully documented and aggressively pursued.

How Roden Law Investigates Truck Accident Cases

Truck accident cases demand an investigative approach that goes far beyond what is required in a standard motor vehicle crash. The Savannah truck accident attorneys at Roden Law deploy a comprehensive investigation strategy designed to uncover every source of liability and every piece of available evidence.

Rapid Evidence Preservation

Within 24 hours of taking a case, Roden Law sends formal spoliation preservation letters to the trucking company, its insurer, and all related parties demanding that they preserve all evidence related to the crash. This includes ECM/black box data, ELD records, driver qualification files, dispatch communications, GPS and telematics data, dash cam and trailer camera footage, drug and alcohol testing records, and vehicle inspection and maintenance logs.

Accident Reconstruction

Roden Law retains independent accident reconstruction experts who analyze physical evidence from the crash scene, vehicle damage patterns, electronic data, and witness testimony to establish exactly how the accident occurred and who was at fault. In cases involving complex multi-vehicle crashes on I-16 or I-95, this expert analysis is often the most important evidence presented at trial.

FMCSA Compliance Audit

The legal team conducts a thorough review of the trucking company's compliance history, including its FMCSA Safety Measurement System (SMS) scores, prior inspection results, out-of-service violations, and any history of enforcement actions. A trucking company with a pattern of safety violations is far more vulnerable to claims of negligent operation — and that history is a matter of public record that Roden Law knows how to access and use effectively.

Building the Full Picture

Additional evidence sources include weigh station records from Georgia Department of Public Safety inspection stations, toll records, fuel purchase receipts that establish the driver's route and timeline, and employment records that reveal whether the company was pushing drivers beyond legal limits. Every detail matters, and overlooking a single source of evidence can mean leaving significant compensation on the table.

Compensation Available in Savannah Truck Accident Cases

Because of the severity of injuries involved, truck accident claims typically involve substantially higher damages than standard motor vehicle accident cases. Roden Law pursues the full range of compensation available under Georgia law, including:

  • Medical expenses — Past, present, and future costs of hospitalization, surgery, rehabilitation, medication, and ongoing care.
  • Lost wages and lost earning capacity — Compensation for income lost during recovery and for diminished ability to earn in the future.
  • Pain and suffering — Physical pain, emotional distress, and diminished quality of life resulting from the injuries.
  • Disability and disfigurement — Compensation for permanent impairments, scarring, and loss of bodily function.
  • Loss of consortium — Damages available to the spouse of a seriously injured victim for loss of companionship and support.
  • Wrongful death damages — Full value of the life of the deceased, including future earning capacity, and funeral and burial expenses.
  • Punitive damages — In cases involving willful misconduct, fraud, or conscious disregard for safety, Georgia law permits punitive damages under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1 to punish the wrongdoer and deter similar conduct.

Trucking companies carry insurance policies with limits that are significantly higher than standard auto policies — often $1 million or more. Roden Law has the experience and resources to litigate against major trucking companies and their national insurers to pursue every dollar of available coverage.

Why Savannah Truck Accident Victims Choose Roden Law

Attorney Eric Roden and the Roden Law team have built a track record of results that speaks for itself. With more than $300 million recovered for injured clients, 5,000+ cases handled, and a 4.9-star average client rating, the firm has established itself as one of the leading personal injury practices in Georgia and South Carolina.

What sets Roden Law apart in truck accident litigation is a combination of resources, preparation, and willingness to go to trial. Trucking companies and their insurers know which law firms will accept a lowball settlement and which firms will take the case to a Chatham County jury. Roden Law has earned a reputation as a firm that prepares every case for trial — and that reputation produces better results for clients at every stage of the process.

The firm operates on a contingency fee basis, meaning clients pay nothing upfront and owe no attorney fees unless Roden Law secures a recovery. With a local office in Savannah, the team is accessible, responsive, and deeply familiar with the courts, roads, and trucking patterns of Chatham County and Southeast Georgia.

Contact Roden Law's Savannah Truck Accident Team

Call (912) 303-5850 today for a free, no-obligation consultation with a Savannah truck accident lawyer. Every case is handled on a contingency fee basis — no fees unless Roden Law wins. The firm is also available toll-free at 1-844-RESULTS.
